articles.title: After launching Vande Bharat sleeper train with 16 coaches, Indian Railways now bets on 24-coach variant of new train with pantry car and features better than Rajdhani Express
articles.summary: After rolling out 16-coach Vande Bharat sleeper trains, Indian Railways is now eyeing a 24-coach train set that will cater to longer distance overnight
articles.body: After rolling out 16-coach Vande Bharat sleeper trains, Indian Railways is now eyeing a 24-coach train set that will cater to longer distance overnight journeys. The Integral Coach Factory (ICF) Chennai has been tasked with manufacturing 50 Vande Bharat sleeper trains that will have 24 coaches.Indian Railways is expected to introduce more than 200 Vande Bharat sleeper trains over the coming years as it seeks to transform long-distance rail travel. Three major manufacturing projects are underway.BEML, with support from ICF, is producing 10 sleeper trainsets, while the Indo-Russian joint venture Kinet has been assigned the task of manufacturing another 120. A consortium of Titagarh and BHEL will produce 80 Vande Bharat sleeper trains. Separately, ICF is preparing to develop a sleeper version of its own.Also Read | Passenger trains being run with slower freight engines as Indian Railways faces locomotives shortage; records show 80-100 cases a month causing delays of several hours24 coach Vande Bharat sleeper train soonSources told TOI that the designs for the new train are being finalised and are expected to be ready in a month’s time. The rollout timeline for the new Vande Bharat sleeper train set is in the first half of 2027, with June 2027 set as a target date.The 24-coach Vande Bharat sleeper trains will be a variant of the existing train design but will include a pantry car.ICF has said in the past that its 24-car Vande Bharat sleeper will be one of the longest sleeper trains being produced in India.The number of toilets on the train will also be increased in the 24-car variant. The ICF version will also include a pantry car, a feature that is absent from the other Vande Bharat sleeper design. This will allow food to be heated and served onboard. The factory is also looking at improving the interiors, although the design work is still underway.Also Read | Delhi-Varanasi in less than 4 hours, Mumbai-Pune in 48 minutes, Chennai-Bengaluru in over 1 hour: Indian Railways bets on seven new bullet train corridors in Rs 16 lakh crore high-speed pushVande Bharat Sleeper Train FeaturesCoach configuration: The prototypes running right now have 16 passenger coaches, comprising 11 AC 3-tier coaches, four AC 2-tier coaches and one AC First Class coach.Speed: The train is designed to operate at 160 kmph and has a testing speed of 180 kmph, placing it in the semi-high-speed category. However, most sections of the Indian Railways network cannot accommodate trains running at such speeds.Berth comfort: Drawing inspiration from European trains, the sleeper variant will feature cushioned berths designed to improve passenger comfort. The arrangement for accessing upper berths has also been redesigned to make climbing easier.Lighting and onboard facilities: The train will have dedicated night lighting, an integrated announcement system with visual displays, CCTV cameras and modular pantry units.Toilets and accessibility: Modern bio-vacuum toilets, similar to those used in aircraft, will be provided. A toilet for disabled passengers will also feature a baby-care station. The AC First Class coach will offer shower facilities with hot water.Safety and energy efficiency: The sleeper train will be fitted with the indigenous KAVACH anti-collision system. Like the chair car versions, it will also use regenerative braking technology to improve energy utilisation.Automatic doors and sealed gangways: The coaches will have automatic interconnecting doors, while fully sealed gangways will help maintain clean air and regulate the temperature inside the train.Passenger amenities: Individual reading lights, charging points, refreshment tables and interiors featuring GFRP panels will be provided in each coach. The train doors will open automatically at designated stations.Monitoring and emergency communication: A Centralised Coach Monitoring System will be installed. Passengers will also be able to communicate with the driver through an emergency communication system.Also Read | Second Vande Bharat sleeper set to launch this month between Bengaluru and Mumbai; cutting travel time from 24 hours to under 16 hours, 30 year wait for faster connectivity between two cities to endYou use AI every day. articles.body: As India accelerates towards a future shaped by innovation and enterprise, a distinguished group of business leaders is emerging at the forefront of change. articles.title: Indian rice exporters move 102,210 tonnes Basmati rice across three vessels to Iraq
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India's rice exporters have arranged shipments of 102,210 metric tonnes of Basmati rice to Iraq across three bulk vessels, aiming to cut
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India's rice exporters have arranged shipments of 102,210 metric tonnes of Basmati rice to Iraq across three bulk vessels, aiming to cut freight costs by 74% amid shipping disruptions, container shortages and rising logistics expenses.The Indian Rice Exporters' Federation (IREF), in collaboration with Singapore-based Eximwala Solutions Pte. Ltd., said the arrangement would bring freight costs down to around $90 per tonne, compared with container-shipping quotations of about $350 per tonne. This would mean a potential saving of $260 per tonne.Based on these quoted rates, the three-vessel programme could generate gross freight savings of about $26.6 million. The actual savings, however, would depend on the final shipping costs and contractual terms.The three vessels are bound for Iraq's Umm Qasr port. The MV LAMAR S, carrying 36,810 tonnes of rice, has reached the port, berthed at Berth No. 3 and begun unloading its cargo, IREF said.The other two vessels: MV LOLO GATE and MV OUTLANDER, have been nominated to carry 25,500 tonnes and 39,900 tonnes, respectively.The initiative comes as exporters face higher freight rates and logistical uncertainty affecting shipments to the Gulf, India's largest regional market for Basmati rice.India exported 4.564 million tonnes of Basmati rice worth Rs 34,284 crore to the Middle East in the financial year ended March 2026, accounting for around 70% of its total Basmati export volume, according to figures cited by IREF.Including non-Basmati varieties, India's rice exports to the region stood at 5.648 million tonnes, valued at Rs 39,657 crore.Saudi Arabia was India's largest Basmati market in the region, with imports worth Rs 8,324 crore in FY2025-26. It was followed by Iran at Rs 6,970 crore, Iraq at Rs 5,583 crore and the United Arab Emirates at Rs 4,132 crore, the federation said.Iraq imported around 764,000 tonnes of Indian Basmati rice during the period, highlighting the importance of competitive freight rates and reliable shipping routes for exporters."The Middle East accounts for nearly 70 per cent of India's Basmati exports, and rising shipping costs directly affect our competitiveness. By targeting a reduction in freight from USD 350 to USD 90 per tonne, we are demonstrating how better logistics can benefit both Indian exporters and overseas buyers. Our objective is to develop similar commercially viable solutions for other Gulf destinations, strengthen India's rice exports and improve returns across the value chain," Dev Garg, national vice president of IREF said, PTI reported.Lower freight costs could help exporters protect profit margins and keep their rice competitively priced in overseas markets. Bulk shipments may also provide an alternative when containers are scarce or expensive.However, the benefits will depend on the availability of bulk vessels, port-handling charges, shipment schedules and whether bulk transport suits individual consignments and buyers.The initiative comes ahead of the Bharat International Rice Conference (BIRC) 2026, scheduled to be held at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi from October 23 to 25.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fed officials are warning of more pain. Many Americans are already feeling it
articles.summary: Four years ago, with inflation at multi-decade highs, then-Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell delivered a blunt message to Americans: Getting inflation under control would come at a cost.
articles.body: Four years ago, with inflation at multi-decade highs, then-Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell delivered a blunt message to Americans: Getting inflation under control would come at a cost. The Fed needed to act “forcefully,” Powell told attendees at a key central banker conference that August. Doing so, he cautioned, would bring “some pain” for consumers. Now, with the Fed back to raising interest rates for the first time in three years, a familiar warning about the economic fallout is resurfacing. Inflation across the country is being driven primarily by fuel prices, which have skyrocketed since the war with Iran broke out in February. The Fed has little control over oil production, but by raising interest rates, it is seeking to prevent higher energy costs from spilling over into other parts of the economy and fueling broader inflation. While this type of supply-driven inflation may be easier to bring under control than the post-pandemic demand-driven inflation, “it won’t be painless either,” Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said last month. For central bankers, the challenge is balancing two competing priorities: keeping inflation in check and preserving a healthy labor market. When price increases become too rapid, the Fed typically raises interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for consumers and businesses. That, in turn, can curb spending and cool demand, easing pressure on prices. But that slowdown can come at a cost to workers, often leading to weaker hiring, fewer job openings, and, in some cases, job losses, as businesses struggle with higher borrowing costs. “Inflation is the disease. And now the Fed comes with a cure: higher interest rates,” Beth Ann Bovino, chief economist at US Bank, said. “I don’t know which is more painful because they both hurt.” Consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of US economic activity, making it a key driver of growth. If Americans pull back — either because prices are eating up more of their budgets or because higher borrowing costs force them to set aside more money for expenses such as a home purchase — the economy could slow. In a worst-case scenario, that pullback could help tip the economy into a recession, Bovino told CNN. For now, though, economic pain isn’t being felt equally. Americans with substantial investments in the stock market, which is hovering near record highs, may be doing just fine. Those who rely more heavily on their paychecks to cover everyday expenses have less of a cushion against rising prices. “Those are the people being hurt,” she said. Patience is a virtue — until it isn’t With the risks of higher interest rates in mind, a growing chorus of Fed officials have recently been advocating for a more patient approach as they tackle the issue of inflation. Rather than trying to get a head start at fighting the potential for more or broader-based inflation, several central bankers have said they’d like more time to observe how economic conditions evolve to get a better idea of how many more rate hikes, if any, are needed. “There is no need for urgency,” New York Fed President John Williams said last month. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson echoed that sentiment. “Any future adjustments in policy should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data, the evolving outlook and the balance of risks,” he said earlier this month. But waiting to act carries risks of its own. With the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge more than a percentage point above its 2% annual target, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack warned that delaying action could make the fight against inflation even more painful. “The longer inflation stays above our objective, the harder it will be for us to bring it back down, and the more pain that individuals and businesses are going to be experiencing,” Hammack said in an August CNBC interview. For the Fed, the challenge is figuring out how much pain the economy can withstand — and which risk is worse: acting too soon or waiting too long. Either way, consumers are likely to pay the price. The September Consumer Price Index report due Wednesday may give officials some valuable clues.

articles.title: Industrialised personalisation
articles.summary: You have been inside the hotel for less than a minute when the waiter at the restaurant door greets you by name.
articles.body: You have been inside the hotel for less than a minute when the waiter at the restaurant door greets you by name. Your usual table, the one by the window, is already laid. Before you open the menu the waiter asks whether it will be the sole again, as it was in March, and you, who eat out a good deal and are hard to impress, feel for a moment like the only guest in the building. You have not said anything. The waiter takes your coat with a small bow and leads the way.In 1911, Frederick Winslow Taylor's ‘The Principles of Scientific Management’ held that the best way to do each job should be worked out in advance, and taught. He wrote, “In the past the man has been first; in the future the system must be first.” Industrial production could then continue seamlessly, with each new worker fitting into the role with ease.The same logic had already moved from products into service, from Fred Harvey's railway restaurants in 1876 to White Castle's hamburger stands in 1921, and in 1948 the McDonald brothers rebuilt their restaurant around a nine-item menu and ran the kitchen like an assembly line. Let's follow a new hire called Dan on his first morning at the McDonald's on Sand Lake Road in Orlando, the chain’s largest outlet. For a moment he is overwhelmed by the arcade, ordering kiosks and a sea of impatient customers. The hour of briefing he was given steadies him. He matches each order number to its table, carries the tray over and says, as taught, “Have a nice meal!” In under a day few can tell he is new. This is industrialised industrialisation, with systems in place but execution still a little rough around the edges.In time, Dan moves to a job at a formal dining room where he trains for a whole week. He moves more fluidly now, personal worries don’t reflect in his demeanour, and his ‘thank you’ with a smile and a gentle nod sounds less rehearsed. The management has done its work well, and it takes a trained eye to see that his manner at the next table is no different.Attention reaches further at Eleven Madison Park, where, Will Guidara has said, whoever greeted you would have looked you up online beforehand. In ‘Unreasonable Hospitality’ he describes training the staff to set every plate so that in the event that a guest turned it over, he’d find the Limoges stamp facing him, right side up.At the Ritz-Carlton, Joseph Michelli reports, guest relations staff share news of arriving guests' anniversaries and celebrations at the daily lineup. You could arrive on a special day and find champagne, a handwritten card and pastries waiting in the room. The Ritz keeps the record of such care in Mystique, a database of guest preferences fed by notes that staff are trained to jot down. If you stayed at one of its hotels, the waiter would likely have drawn on it.Industrialised personalisation, in the world of service, means a system set down so completely that anyone properly trained can replicate it and make an experience feel personal.Dan leads you to the window. When the sole comes, it is cooked the way it was in March.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Two Americans win Nobel prize for models to tackle economic downturns
articles.summary: American professors Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford have won the 2026 Nobel prize in economics for developing new economic models that help governments and central banks stabilize their economies to minimize the impact of external shocks.
articles.body: American professors Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford have won the 2026 Nobel prize in economics for developing new economic models that help governments and central banks stabilize their economies to minimize the impact of external shocks. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the prize in Stockholm on Monday. “The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy’s peaks and troughs,” the academy said in a statement, adding that their models have been “extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us.” Hall, born in Palo Alto, California in 1943, is a professor at Stanford University. Woodford, born in Chicopee, Massachusetts in 1955, is a professor at Columbia University. They will each receive 6 million Swedish kronor ($598,000) in prize money. Their work “has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” noted John Hassler, the chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences. “With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” he added. Rather than analyzing links between so-called “macroeconomic” variables such as inflation, production and consumption, Hall and Woodford looked to “microeconomics” to understand how the decisions of individuals and households can affect the economy. Central to their models was the insight that households and businesses are “forward-looking” when making decisions about savings or how to price products. Governments and central banks can influence this view of the future when communicating their plans for fiscal and monetary policy respectively and so “move the economy in the right direction,” the academy said. The prize, officially known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, was not instituted by Alfred Nobel. It was established by Sweden’s central bank in 1968 and is awarded in memory of Nobel. The number of individuals who have been awarded the prize now totals 101, only three of whom have been women. Fewer than half of the prizes awarded since 1969 have gone to one laureate only. The economics prize concludes this year’s Nobel awards. South African judge and human rights pioneer Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday. A day prior, Canadian writer Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in literature.

articles.title: Direct selling in India is now a Rs 23,522-crore business with 91 lakh sellers: ADSEI report
articles.summary: India's direct selling industry clocked sales of Rs 23,522 crore in 2024-25 and is set to cross Rs 25,000 crore in the current fiscal, according to a
articles.body: India's direct selling industry clocked sales of Rs 23,522 crore in 2024-25 and is set to cross Rs 25,000 crore in the current fiscal, according to a report released on Monday at Bharat Mandapam by the Association of Direct Selling Entities of India (ADSEI) and its research partner Kantar.The industry has grown from Rs 16,776 crore in 2019-20, a compound annual growth rate of about 7%, while the number of active direct sellers rose from 72 lakh to 91 lakh over the same period. Women make up 47% of them, or roughly 43 lakh sellers. The report places India 11th among the world's top 15 direct selling markets, worth an estimated $2.8-3 billion.ADSEI president Dr Sanjeev Kumar said the report established "with credible quantified and qualitative data" what the sector contributes, chiefly "livelihoods for more than 91 lakh people, nearly half of them women".Wellness products alone account for about 61% of sales; add cosmetics and personal care, and the share rises to 86%.Maharashtra is the largest market at Rs 3,058 crore, followed by West Bengal (Rs 2,376 crore) and Uttar Pradesh (Rs 1,788 crore). The top 10 states together contribute about 70% of national sales.A survey of 572 sellers conducted for the report found that 65% depend on direct selling as their only source of income, and 73% described their month-on-month earnings as very or somewhat consistent. Those with other sources of income reported average additional earnings of about Rs 18,000 a month. Some 69% of sellers are between 25 and 44 years old."Behind the Rs 23,522 crore are 91 lakh Indians who decided to bet on themselves," said Gautam Bali, patron, ADSEI. "But too many still leave before their business finds its feet. Sharper training, stronger governance and an uncompromising commitment to the consumer are how we ensure that everyone who joins with hope stays to build something lasting."The report credits the Consumer Protection (Direct Selling) Rules, 2021 with formalising the sector, and 83% of sellers surveyed viewed the impact of policy favourably. Their wish list for the government includes easier access to bank accounts and loans (61%), uniform central regulation across states (53%) and a dedicated regulator along the lines of Sebi or Irdai (42%).The numbers also show how far the industry has to go. Per-capita spending on direct selling in India is about $2, against $8-12 in the lower rungs of the global top 10. Breaking into that group would require the market to reach $6-7 billion, growing 12-14% a year, nearly twice its current pace. The business is also concentrated: six companies with revenue of Rs 1,000 crore or more hold about 68% of industry revenue, while over 400 firms earn less than Rs 10 crore each.Puneet Avasthi, director at Kantar, said the industry was "transitioning from a participation-led growth model to one increasingly driven by productivity, value creation, and ecosystem maturity"You use AI every day. articles.title: Robert Price was sitting on a $1 trillion frozen goldmine. Then Dr. Phil got involved
articles.summary: The Texas wildcatter recorded a podcast with Dr. Phil about gaining exclusive drilling rights in Greenland. The locals were furious.
articles.body: Robert Price hadn’t noticed the 10-foot-tall wartime photo of his dad behind him. “That’s him, yeah. He was stationed…” The Texas wildcatter stopped, his eyes welling up with tears. He gave a cautious laugh and looked back up at the photo. “Um,” Price started again, his voice wavering. “He was stationed in Greenland for three years at a weather station.” Price was sitting in the middle of a decked-out studio, recording a podcast hosted by Phil McGraw, aka Dr. Phil, the frequent “Oprah Winfrey Show” guest turned TV host turned vocal surrogate for President Donald Trump. The veteran oilman had gained exclusive drilling rights in Jameson Land, a remote part of Greenland right at the Arctic Circle – and what he believes is the world’s last frontier oil project. As many as 13 billion barrels of crude, worth more than $1 trillion at today’s prices, were frozen deep within the very same stretch of frozen land that Price’s weatherman father was deployed to monitor during World War II. It was oil that the world desperately needed, with war raging in the Middle East and global crude stockpiles plunging by 2 billion barrels to reach critical lows over the past seven months. Price wanted to tell the world all about it, and Dr. Phil was going to help him do it. “My dad would be really proud,” he said on the podcast. The emotional interview may have undone Price’s dream. Greenlanders, already on edge about Trump’s ambition to control Greenland, were furious. Local regulators withdrew their backing for the project. Price cut ties with Dr. Phil and is trying to make peace. In an interview with CNN, he said politics aren’t at play here. This is about helping Greenland benefit from its natural riches. “This is about bringing capital to Greenland. It has nothing to do with the Trump administration,” Price told CNN. “Politics will come and go, but our project will be there for a long period of time.” Price hopes he can salvage the massive and expensive project by doing some serious damage control. His company, Greenland Energy, said in a recent press release it would take no shortcuts, and it would continue the painstaking regulatory process “one day and one step at a time.” Another misstep could keep all that potential oil locked under the frozen surface forever. Promise of riches Price has oil in his blood. His grandfather died in an oil rig fire. His father was raised in Cushing, Oklahoma, the pipeline crossroads of the world. And Price spent his decades-long career getting land for oil majors to drill. But he had never seen an opportunity like this. Price knows it sounds nutty. His wells are hidden miles under an ice sheet in a remote part of Greenland with no way in or out, all winter long. Price remembers his father telling him stories about dogsleds, skiing, fishing, eating seal, hunting and the like. He still has 50 letters that his father wrote home to Price’s grandmother from his remote station in the arctic. But he says the gamble is worth it: This isn’t a complicated extraction project like the tar sands of Canada, Brazilian pre-salt oil or even Texas Permian Basin horizontal fracking. It’s old-fashioned, drill-straight-down-until-you-strike-oil stuff, which means if he strikes oil (Price says “when” he strikes oil), he can drill considerably more profitably than those projects. “Greenland is a beautiful, extraordinary place,” Price told CNN. “And to tell the story, not only of Greenland, but of the Greenlandic people and what our potential discovery might be, is important to me.” Price argues that Greenland’s potential oil riches would become a boon for its inhabitants. But convincing Greenlanders – who endured threats this year by President Donald Trump to annex or buy their land – of the wisdom of allowing an American oil company to profit from their natural resources may be difficult. So when an opportunity arose more than 10 years ago to get a license to drill there, Price jumped at the chance. Arco, a company that had surveyed the basin starting in the 1970s, put its Greenland drilling licenses and seismic surveys up for auction. The company had spent three decades and $250 million preparing to exploit the oil in two gigantic wells below Jameson Land, a remote part of Greenland right at the Arctic Circle. Arco built an airstrip nearby. But the economics never made sense for Arco, and in 1990, the company gave up on the project. It never drilled there. Now, the economics have changed entirely: Oil is around $100 a barrel, and drilling technology has vastly improved over the past several decades. Price sniffed an opportunity. Except a British company, 80 Mile, beat him to the punch. So Price reached out with an offer: 80 Mile would work with the Greenland government to nail down the drilling rights, and Price would bring in all the financing, drilling equipment and workers. Price would enter a joint venture with 80 Mile and take up to a 70% interest in the wells. That meant Price got an opportunity to follow in his father’s footsteps and go to Greenland – a dream he says he had long held since hearing those stories of how his father secretively helped deliver critical weather information to the Allied Forces in their fight against the Nazis. Price set up the financing, getting some big-named backers, including mega hedge fund Citadel and its CEO Ken Griffin. Greenland Energy went public in March through a SPAC. As recently as this past spring, it seemed all systems go: 80 Mile had completed its permitting paperwork in May 2025. The Greenland government asked the company to drill in the winter to reduce the potential environmental impact and to drill only one of its wells. An Albertan rig was ready to set sail from Montreal to Nuuk. And then Dr. Phil shared the news about his Greenland Energy documentary. The Dr. Phil Podcast To tell his story, Price chose Dr. Phil. Throughout the 44-minute episode, McGraw interviewed Price about the project and previewed future episodes of the adventure, which he titled “Frozen Gold: Oil’s Final Frontier.” The news of any US company exploiting the region’s resources would necessarily be politically charged, after Trump announced in his inaugural address and repeatedly throughout his second term that the United States would control the territory – suggesting at times that the United States could even take the land by force without Greenlanders’ consent. Trump’s “less-than-sensitive language” wasn’t helpful to Greenland Energy’s specific project, but his comments shone a light on Greenland’s importance to the Western world, to the United States and to NATO, said Greenland Energy Chair Larry Swets. That helped increase investor awareness and, with it, capital, he told CNN. Still, Greenlanders got riled up over Greenland Energy’s connection to Griffin (a well-heeled Trump supporter), Carol Craig (who runs a company working on Trump’s Golden Dome missile defense project that Trump wants stationed in Greenland), and the splashy adventure documentary from McGraw. The Greenland government, which had been working closely with 80 Mile for years, slammed the brakes. The government said Greenland Energy had attempted to set sail under an expired permit. The company decided to air-lift equipment instead, which really got Greenland authorities upset – they viewed the gambit as an effort to bypass regulations. Last month, Greenland Energy announced it would delay its operations until October. A week later, the company said it was suspending all drilling until 2027. The company also paused its relationship with McGraw. Representatives for McGraw did not respond to a request for comment. Choosing Dr. Phil may have been a mistake. But Price doesn’t see it that way. “Regardless of what his political affiliations are, he is a compelling storyteller,” Price said. The whole premise of the documentary was that “there is an amazing story to tell,” added Swets. “Not just about energy and oil, but about the geopolitics and the people that are in the middle of that,” he told CNN. “It’s regrettable that maybe we didn’t take enough time to have Greenlanders come alongside (the documentary), rather than feel like it was pushed on them.” Why Greenland matters Drilling in the Arctic Circle is not for the faint-hearted. Between 40 and 50 workers would need to be helicoptered in for the winter with an on-staff nurse, a blood bank and two chefs – because once temperatures plummet and the ice sheet moves in, there’s no easy way out. Every onsite worker will be required to carry a gun to protect themselves from polar bears. Those are the risks that wildcatters like Price are willing to take on. “This is about shoring up a potential supply of oil on into the future,” Price said. The war in Iran made clear that the world needs alternative energy sources – including renewable energy but also easily drillable oil projects outside the Middle East. The shale revolution has made the United States the world’s largest energy producer, but some oil industry analysts fear Texas’ Permian Basin is close to exhausting its supply of tier 1 oil – the most easily accessible and profitably extracted crude. No one knows exactly when that might happen; many think the Permian has another few years or even a decade of tier 1 oil left. But oil majors aren’t waiting. ExxonMobil’s massive oil well discovery off the coast of Guyana is already nearing 1 million barrels of production a day. Chevron and the United States are placing massive bets on Venezuela. Price’s expectation of achieving profitability at around $20 means there’s enormous potential reward in Greenland. Even though Arco confirmed the presence of the massive subterranean wells decades ago, drilling doesn’t always yield anything. “There’s clearly risk in doing exploration,” acknowledged Swets. “We know the oil is there, but we don’t know if we can get it out… The only way to get new information is to drill a well.” Greenland has a long history of failed attempts to extract its oil, including from big companies like BP and Shell and many smaller companies who weren’t able to get much of anything out of the ground. In 2021, Greenland stopped offering drilling licenses – only allowing grandfathered licenses, such as Greenland Energy’s, to exploit the resources. If they’re available. “After we get the first well drilled, then we can decide how to move forward after that,” Price said. He’ll have to wait until next year to find out. At least.

articles.title: When AI goes rogue, who should get sued?
articles.summary: The AI industry has been buzzing with concern about potentially catastrophic risks to humanity — a hum of anxiety that’s grown louder as Anthropic prepares to make its stock market debut next month.
articles.body: The AI industry has been buzzing with concern about potentially catastrophic risks to humanity — a hum of anxiety that’s grown louder as Anthropic prepares to make its stock market debut next month. But companies building AI models like Claude and ChatGPT face a more immediate and prosaic risk: They’re likely to get sued. A lot. AI companies have so far avoided major lawsuits over recent incidents in which they’ve failed to keep AI agents — systems capable of working autonomously with little oversight — contained to their testing environments. But some legal experts and policymakers say it’s pretty clear: The companies can and should be held responsible “The question of ‘how is the law going to apply to this?’ is a lot easier to answer if you see (AI) as it is, and not as this hypothetical thing that many in the industry are proposing it might someday be,” said Kristen Thomasen, associate professor at University of Windsor and an expert in robotics law. “The law has dealt with new technologies for as long as it has existed.” The AI industry often refers to the breakout incidents as the technology going “rogue” — language that some critics say is designed to amplify the companies’ claims that their technology is so powerful that even its creators struggle to contain it. It may also be a tactic to try to shield themselves from responsibility and future legal claims, Thomasen said. Still, she said, the liability questions around AI models have a simple answer: “It’s a thing that this company is putting out into the world. If it does harm, there are laws that regulate that.” The cost of ‘rogue’ meddling So far, the real-world harms done by rogue bots have been far from calamitous but nonetheless costly for the organizations they’ve infiltrated. Last week, the nonprofit that operates Wikipedia said it had found evidence of unauthorized OpenAI agents attempting to make “potentially malicious edits” to some pages and pummeling it with so much traffic that they may have triggered a partial outage. The investigation “stopped work inside key parts of the organization for us to focus on this,” Eric Mill, product manager for safety and security at Wikimedia, told CNN. “We put our very best people on it… and it’s a pretty messy process.” Wikimedia launched its investigation this summer as global alarm grew over the Hugging Face attack and dozens of other instances of internal AI models breaking out of their testing environments to hack other computer systems. Meta and Anthropic also disclosed that their test models have hacked into other systems without authorization. The Wikimedia probe is significant in part because of what didn’t happen: There was no catastrophic, existential threat to humanity of the sort that AI executives often allude to. But the cost — more than two weeks of work carried out by the leading engineers at a global, $200 million-plus organization — was real. Wikimedia isn’t pushing any one policy or technological solution, and Mill said the organization is in communication with OpenAI about its findings. (OpenAI didn’t respond to CNN’s request for comment.) But the nonprofit hopes these incidents are a wake-up call for AI developers. “AI companies are not doing enough to secure their systems and protect the public from the harm they cause,” Wikimedia said in its blog post last week. “That burden is falling onto everyone else, including smaller organizations.” ‘Long overdue accountability’ Anthropic, which is preparing to go public next month in one of the largest IPOs in history, disclosed in a regulatory filing that because the legal framework around AI is “unsettled,” those agents’ actions could expose the company to “significant and unpredictable” lawsuits, according to a copy of the document viewed by Reuters. The potential litigation onslaught isn’t just a headache for company lawyers or a quandary for academics — it could also become a major drag on Anthropic’s bottom line. Litigation costs are a financial drain for any company, but it could become especially problematic for Anthropic, which is burning through cash faster than it can bring it in. The company tore through $42 billion last year while bringing in just $4.6 billion in revenue, according to the document seen by Reuters. The CEOs of both Anthropic and OpenAI have argued for new regulations tailored to the industry. Dario Amodei recently penned an essay arguing that companies “pace the frontier” and foster international cooperation on safety protocols. But the rival AI firms have diverged slightly on the liability question. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman earlier this year favored an Illinois bill that would limit when AI labs can be held liable, even when their products cause “critical harm.” (Anthropic came out against it.) And while Altman endorsed Amodei’s “pace the frontier” proposal, he also told POLITICO earlier week that his worldview isn’t perfectly aligned with his rival’s: OpenAI believes “the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology,” he said. Altman also told the news site that “if something goes wrong with our models during training, there’s gonna be some version of that we need to be responsible for.” An Anthropic spokesperson told CNN the company sees liability laws as a backstop, rather than a substitute, for safety regulations. Anthropic has never proposed exemptions from existing liability laws, the spokesperson added. Policymakers on the left and the right have sought to cut through some of the more nuanced questions of future regulation and underscore the legal liabilities AI is already subject to. Lina Khan, the former Federal Trade Commission chair under President Joe Biden, has become a prominent challenger to AI executives, arguing on X that “we shouldn’t let discussions about new legal regimes distract from the fact that there’s no AI exemption from laws already on the books.” Meanwhile, Republican Senator Josh Hawley, alongside Democratic counterpart Chris Murphy, introduced a bill last week that seeks to ensure “AI agent operators and developers are held liable for hacking incidents.” “What these companies need is not more power… but some long-overdue accountability,” Hawley wrote in a Washington Post op-ed. “One way to give that to them is to let the people they harm sue them in court.” A design question Legal experts who spoke to CNN said that while product liability and consumer protection issues aren’t new, there will inevitably be some nuanced aspects of the technology that will ultimately fall on the courts to rule on. “We’ve seen these sorts of issues with gun safety or with cigarettes or other issues, and it’s really interesting — what analogy will the courts seize onto?” said Frank Pasquale, a Cornell law professor and an expert on AI law. One of the bigger questions Pasquale expect courts to grapple with is design. For example, he said, imagine if a manufacturer made a car with sharp swords at the end of it, and then someone drove that car into a pedestrian. The logical response is pretty simple: Don’t design something with swords attached to it. It’s similar with AI products, he said: Don’t design something that tries a password 50 times or more. Make sure it contains high level instructions that would override any user’s effort to misuse it. “I think it’s very hard for (AI companies) to say, ‘Oh, it can do a billion different things but we can’t control it.’” Pasquale said. “That doesn’t make sense to me because if it can do all these things, then you can also have meta-rules, or rules for the for the rules, that would that would prevent it from doing certain bad things.” —CNN’s Hadas Gold contributed reporting.

articles.title: Retail inflation at almost 2-year high at 5.54% in September, driven by food prices surge
articles.summary: Retail inflation moved closer to the Reserve Bank of India’s upper tolerance limit of 6 per cent in September, rising to 5.54 per cent from 4.83 per cent
articles.body: Retail inflation moved closer to the Reserve Bank of India’s upper tolerance limit of 6 per cent in September, rising to 5.54 per cent from 4.83 per cent in August as food prices recorded a sharper increase. Food inflation climbed to 7.74 per cent during the month, against 5.97 per cent in August, according to data released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation on Monday.The September reading marked the highest inflation rate since the introduction of the new Consumer Price Index (CPI) series with a 2024 base year. Compared with the earlier 2012-base series, the revised index uses an updated framework to measure changes in household prices. On a comparable historical measure, inflation was at its highest level since late 2024.The pressure was more pronounced in rural India, where retail inflation reached 6.08 per cent, up from 5.24 per cent in August. The corresponding rate for urban areas rose to 4.88 per cent from 4.31 per cent. Rural food inflation stood at 8.06 per cent, compared with 7.18 per cent in urban areas.Among individual items, onion prices saw the steepest increase, with inflation surging to 108.09 per cent in September from 48.78 per cent in the previous month. Ginger prices rose 62.85 per cent year-on-year, while garlic inflation accelerated to 54.62 per cent. Lemon prices also saw a sharp increase, with inflation reaching 36.41 per cent, against 15.15 per cent in August. Silver jewellery recorded inflation of 87.80 per cent.Price movements were not uniform across the basket. Potato prices remained 11.50 per cent lower than a year earlier, while tomato prices declined 8.62 per cent. Motor cars and jeeps recorded a 4.51 per cent fall, and prices of lady's finger and coconut were down 4.48 per cent and 3.99 per cent, respectively.Beyond food, restaurants and accommodation services recorded inflation of 9.36 per cent, while the personal care, social protection and miscellaneous goods and services category saw prices rise 13.75 per cent. Inflation in food and beverages stood at 7.36 per cent. Health recorded a comparatively modest increase of 1.40 per cent, while housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels registered inflation of 2.74 per cent.Among states and Union territories, Puducherry reported the highest combined inflation at 6.86 per cent, followed by Tamil Nadu at 6.81 per cent, Odisha at 6.70 per cent, Madhya Pradesh at 6.68 per cent and Telangana at 6.64 per cent.The September figures are provisional. articles.title: IIT-Bombay report recommends cutting UPI MDR from 0.4% to 0.08%; says banks should give up their share as they earned Rs 4.85 lakh crore from CASA deposits in FY26
articles.summary: With a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on merchant UPI transactions being announced above Rs 2,000, professors at IIT-Bombay have come out with a report
articles.body: With a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on merchant UPI transactions being announced above Rs 2,000, professors at IIT-Bombay have come out with a report proposing reducing the MDR to 0.08% from 0.40%.The report's authors, Ashish Das, a professor in IIT-Bombay's Department of Mathematics, and Pragya Das, a former RBI official, have argued that third-party application providers (TPAPs), such as PhonePe and Google Pay, as well as payment service providers (PSPs), which are predominantly banks, should receive compensation for the services they provide.The study recommends setting the MDR share for TPAPs at 0.06%, lower than the 0.08% proposed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), while keeping the PSP share unchanged at 0.02%.Under the existing arrangement, banks that issue and acquire transactions collectively receive the bulk of the revenue, with a 70% share split between them. The report has called for this allocation to be eliminated, arguing that banks already benefit from the lower interest rates paid to current and savings account depositors.According to the study, banks recorded a net interest margin (NIM) of more than Rs 4.85 lakh crore from current account and savings account (CASA) deposits in FY26. It described this as "large and disproportionate" compensation for offering a limited range of services free of charge."Banks earn substantial interest margins from the CASA depositors. They should use the same towards running and improving the UPI ecosystem and not rely on MDR revenue sharing from offline transactions," it said according to PTI.The report further suggested that banks could set aside around 3% of the funds, estimated at Rs 15,000 crore, that CASA depositors forgo through lower interest earnings. This money could be used to operate and upgrade the UPI ecosystem instead of depending on MDR revenue sharing.It also urged the RBI and the government to direct banks to treat UPI as an essential service that must be offered to remain in the banking business. The report compared this with the adoption of Core Banking Solutions (CBS), which has since become a necessity for banks.The study also questioned the reasonableness of transaction charges on high-value UPI payments. A charge of Rs 300 on a peer-to-merchant transaction worth Rs 75,000 or more, it said, "raises a vital question of reasonableness of fixing such a high cap as service charge".The report pointed out that RBI regulations require service charges to remain broadly in line with the average cost of providing the service.Digital payment fee proposed for online purchasesThe report has recommended introducing a 'digital payment fee' on online merchant transactions involving purchases of goods or services from e-commerce companies.It noted that many merchants covered by the UPI MDR framework already levy charges on transactions exceeding Rs 2,000 and also accept credit card payments. To address concerns that credit card users are placing an additional burden on peer-to-merchant (P2M) UPI users, the authors recommended lowering credit card MDR.The report also called on the RBI to reconsider the "retention of generous fee free ATM withdrawal allowances". It argued that maintaining such allowances was difficult to justify when consumers have access to convenient digital payment options.In addition, the study recommended continuing the Payments Infrastructure Development Fund (PIDF). According to the report, extending the fund would help payment aggregators bring more merchants onto digital payment platforms.The report questioned the rationale for applying the credit card MDR structure to UPI transactions, stating that there appears to be "no rationale for the credit card's MDR model to be used for UPI". It added that if an 'ad valorem' fee structure, under which charges are calculated as a proportion of the transaction value, is introduced for UPI, the maximum charge should be limited to Rs 40 per transaction.UPI, the report noted, is a public digital infrastructure that has made payments considerably more convenient for users while improving economic productivity. The long-term economic gains generated by the platform outweigh the additional revenue that could be collected through fees on merchant transactions, according to the paper titled 'UPI at a Crossroads: Reintroducing the MDR'.The authors warned that introducing the proposed MDR framework in its current form could weaken public confidence in UPI. They emphasised that the payment system should not become a source of dissatisfaction among users. The report also recommended making it mandatory for merchants with annual turnover of Rs 50 crore or more to offer UPI as a payment option.The paper proposed generating revenue for the UPI ecosystem by limiting the charges to merchants whose annual turnover exceeds Rs 50 crore, equivalent to around Rs 4 crore a month. Such a structure would account for approximately 90% of the MDR proposed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), it said.The report also observed that NPCI could introduce a reasonable charge, within the existing legal framework, on all online person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions.What does the NPCI's MDR circular say?Under a circular issued by NPCI last month, a merchant discount rate of 0.4% will apply to person-to-merchant UPI transactions exceeding Rs 2,000.The fee will be borne by merchants rather than consumers. For transactions worth Rs 75,000 or more, the charge will be capped at Rs 300.Transfers between individuals and most routine payments to merchants will continue to be free. However, transactions above Rs 2,000 for essential services, including railways, telecom, fuel and insurance, will attract a flat fee of Rs 5 per transaction.A lower MDR of 0.02% will apply to capital market transactions, including mutual fund investments and stockbroking, with the fee capped at Rs 300.NPCI, which operates the UPI platform, issued the circular on September 15, introducing MDR on specified UPI transactions. The stated objective of the move is to establish a sustainable revenue model for the digital payments ecosystem.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Tesla chart watchers eye $400-mark as key level for breakout
articles.summary: A late summer bounce in Tesla Inc. shares contrasts with bearish indicators, leaving the market with questions about which direction the electric vehicle mak...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- A late summer bounce in Tesla Inc. shares contrasts with bearish indicators, leaving the market with questions about which direction the electric vehicle maker's stock will head next.

Tesla stock has advanced 28% from a late-July low, which followed the company's report of a quarterly profit miss and swelling capital expenditures.

Still, shares are down 15% in 2026 so far and have underperformed the benchmark S&P 500's 14% ascent. And technical indicators are also muddled as the company remains years away from achieving its artificial intelligence goals.

"This very near term range captures the stage of purgatory the stock is in longer term," said John Kolovos, chief technical strategist at Macro Risk Advisors.

Tesla's stock price now sits between the 50- and 200-day moving averages, levels that serve as popular gauges of a security's momentum. This position represents a clash between recent strength and potential longer-term sluggishness.

"To keep it real simple, a breakout above the 200-DMA with follow through above $400 resistance would resolve things positively," according to Kolovos. "Conversely, a break under the 50-DMA with follow through under $345 would resolve the range negatively."

Evercore ISI head of technical analysis Rich Ross said that an upswing will be largely contingent on Tesla climbing above the 200-day level and making its way back to $400 per share.

"Tesla above $400 sounds, looks, and trades a lot better," Ross said.

Tesla stock has steadily fallen from December's record high as the market's enthusiasm for its AI products fizzled. According to Ross, without a strong breakout, "we have to operate as if the downtrend is still intact."

The technical uncertainty arises as the Elon Musk-led firm attempts to expand beyond the auto business and dominate the world of physical AI.

JC O'Hara, chief technical strategist at Roth Capital Partners, said Tesla's shares may be poised for a sharp move, and a fundamental catalyst could be necessary to break the stalemate and decide their future path.

Tesla will report third-quarter earnings later this month, and investors hope the company's AI transformation is on track toward unlocking larger profits and steeper share gains.

articles.title: Microsoft reveals Maia 300 AI chip as it works to reduce dependence on Nvidia, AMD
articles.summary: Microsoft has launched its new Maia 300 AI chip.
articles.body:
Microsoft ( MSFT ) has debuted its latest AI chip, the Azure Maia 300, as it looks to reduce its reliance on third-party processors from the likes of Nvidia ( NVDA ) and AMD ( AMD ).

Unveiled at the OCP Global Summit 2026 in San Jose on Monday, the Maia 300 will join Microsoft's Maia 200 and Maia 100 chips as part of what the company said will be multigigawatt deployments beginning next year.

The Windows maker said that will make its Maia chips the "primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services."

The company said Maia 300 provides 40% more tokens per megawatt than "leading GPU-based systems," a clear swipe at Nvidia, and that a 96-chip rack offers seven times the rack-scale token throughput of Microsoft's Maia 200.

Tokens are a basic unit of measurement in AI systems that can represent parts of words, images, and videos.

The more tokens per megawatt, the more efficient an AI rack.

The Maia 200 chip currently powers its Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, as well as OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) models, Microsoft's MAI models, and open-source models. That provides 1.7 times more tokens per watt for AI capabilities in Microsoft's Teams, Copilot, and Cowork software versus other GPU-based systems, the company said.

Microsoft and fellow hyperscaler peers Amazon ( AMZN ), Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Meta ( META ), as well as AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ), either already offer or are working on their own custom chips.

Doing so acts as a hedge against becoming overdependent on processors from Nvidia and AMD. Producing their own semiconductors also allows companies to tailor them to their specific needs.

That's a potential problem for Nvidia, which regularly generates upwards of 50% of its quarterly revenue from hyperscalers.

On top of that, Amazon and Google now rent out their custom chips to third-party customers, a direct threat to Nvidia's business. What's more, Amazon is looking into selling chips for customers to install in their own data centers rather than running them from Amazon's own facilities.

That doesn't necessarily mean hyperscalers will stop purchasing Nvidia chips entirely. Customers still want access to a number of chips for different workloads, meaning the Amazons and Microsofts of the world will need to continue stocking up on the most in-demand processors.

articles.title: Google debuts $180 Fitbit Edge tracker in continued health push
articles.summary: The Edge, which replaces the Fitbit Charge 6, offers consumers another vehicle for trying out the recently revamped Google Health app.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Google introduced an updated premium fitness band with a screen, a device that's a cross between smartwatches and more discreet health gadgets that offer continuous tracking.The $180 Fitbit Edge, announced Monday, has an oval, 1.34-inch display that makes it look like a smartwatch, even though it's a purpose-built fitness gadget. The device has a replaceable battery — a first for Fitbit — that's rated to last a week at a time and can recharge to a day's worth of power in five minutes. Other additions include automatic workout detection, an altimeter and wellness features such as proactive health monitoring and the ability to track changes in insulin resistance.

The device comes in four colors — obsidian, canyon, fog and olive green — and is available for preorder now, with shipments starting Oct. 27. A special-edition Stephen Curry version, named for the professional basketball player and Google adviser, is being offered in select countries for $220.

The new device gives Google another way to promote its redesigned health app, which debuted in May and replaced the old Fitbit user experience. While the platform is free to use, upgrading to Google Health Premium for $10 a month or $100 a year unlocks more advanced features, including a conversational AI fitness coach that offers sleep insights and personalized recommendations. Fitbit Edge buyers will get three months of the paid service at no extra charge.

The Edge succeeds the Fitbit Charge 6, which launched in 2023 with a similarly tall screen. As part of its announcement Monday, Google said it will discontinue the Charge line to focus on the Edge, Pixel Watch and the Fitbit Air, the screenless tracker it introduced in May alongside the overhauled Google Health app. Other companies such as Whoop Inc. and Oura Inc. also offer AI health assistants, but Google stands out as one one of a few brands alongside Apple Inc. and Garmin Ltd. offering a meaningful selection of features without requiring a subscription.

In addition to common sports, automatic workout detection on the Edge applies to activities that don't fit a typical definition of exercise, like chores or pushing a stroller. The device also has several health tools that are standard across most smartwatches and premium fitness trackers, including continuous heart rate tracking and the ability to detect irregular rhythms. It can also send alerts when it logs significant heart-rate changes.

articles.title: Starbucks is ‘not buying Chipotle’ after report it explored a deal
articles.summary: Starbucks said that it would not be moving to buy Chipotle Mexican Grill, after a report days earlier said the coffeehouse chain had evaluated the prospect.
articles.body: Starbucks said Monday that it would not be moving to buy Chipotle Mexican Grill, after a report last week said the coffeehouse chain had evaluated the prospect. “As a matter of policy, we don’t comment on rumors and speculation, but we want to be clear we are not buying Chipotle,” a Starbucks spokesperson told NBC News in an email. “Our team is laser focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy,” they said, while adding that the company looked forward to sharing its latest financial results later in October. The announcement from Starbucks came after the Financial Times reported Thursday that “Starbucks has explored a takeover of Chipotle Mexican Grill.” The report also said that it had hired advisers to work on a takeover proposal for Chipotle. Starbucks responded to the report later Thursday by issuing a statement that did not definitively address the status of its interest in Chipotle. A deal between Starbucks and Chipotle would have been transformative for the restaurant and fast-casual dining sector. It would have also reunited Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol with Chipotle, the company he led until late 2024. In the immediate aftermath of the FT report, Starbucks shares fell, while Chipotle’s stock surged sharply higher. But over the past year, the two companies have been on different trajectories. Starbucks is in the midst of a vast turnaround program, which Niccol has touted in recent weeks as delivering progress. Over the past year, Starbucks shares have risen 15%. On the other hand, Chipotle’s shares have plunged 20% over the past 12 months. Both companies are grappling with broadly higher prices for consumers and lagging traffic and are trying to revive sales. Chipotle did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday.

articles.title: AMD launches Helion rack server for agentic AI
articles.summary: AMD is diving further into the agentic AI race with its new AMD Helion data center rack server.
articles.body:
AMD ( AMD ) is diving further into the agentic AI race with its new AMD Helion data center rack server.

Unveiled at the OCP Global Summit in San Jose, Calif., on Monday, Helion is designed to be outfitted with various configurations of CPUs and GPUs based on customers' needs.

The Helion is intended to serve as a reference design for AMD partners and clients, providing instructions for building the platforms.

The company said the server can be fully equipped with its sixth-generation EPYC CPUs for handling agentic AI tasks and servers, or configured with a collection of CPUs and its Instinct MI350P GPUs , which would serve as an all-purpose AI platform.

"Agentic AI is not one single workload. Agents are required for enterprise applications to running code and coordinating complex workflows," Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager of compute and enterprise AI at AMD, said in a statement.

"To do that takes optimized compute and infrastructure that can adapt to different workloads. With AMD Helion, we are bringing AMD EPYC performance, open software and flexible rack designs together so our partners can build systems around customer needs and make efficient use of available power," he added.

The move allows AMD to better compete with rival Nvidia ( NVDA ), which offers its own rack server reference designs, including its NVL72 servers.

AMD, like the rest of the chip industry, continues to benefit from the AI boom. The company topped analysts' estimates on the top and bottom lines during its most recent earnings report and provided a better-than-anticipated outlook for the current quarter.

Earnings per share rose 245%, while revenue climbed 50% to $11.5 billion.

Nvidia, however, continues to dominate in terms of sales, bringing in $96.2 billion in the prior quarter.

AMD stock, though, has outperformed Nvidia's over the last year, climbing roughly 182% year to date. Nvidia stock is up 25% in the same time period.

articles.title: A handful of tech stocks are masking an ugly S&P 500 problem
articles.summary: Without gains from Nvidia, Micron, and a few other high-profile tech stocks, the S&P 500 would be looking ugly.
articles.body:
Thank goodness for the likes of Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron ( MU ), and a few other high-profile tech stocks in the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ).

Without their strong gains , the S&P 500 would be looking ugly — and far from hovering at record highs .

About 84% of S&P 500 stocks are now trading at least 10% below their all-time highs, according to new analysis from the Kobeissi Letter. The Real Estate ( XLRE ) sector leads the pullback, with 97% of its stocks down at least 10%, followed by Materials ( XLB ) at 96%, Utilities ( XLU ) at 94%, and Consumer Discretionary ( XLY ) at 92%.

Pressure in these spaces likely reflects concerns about earnings from companies exposed to high interest rates, notably in housing and retail. Energy, meanwhile, has held up relatively better, with 62% of stocks in the sector more than 10% below their all-time highs, followed by Healthcare ( XLV ) at 70% and Technology ( XLK ) at 72%. What's more, 59% of S&P 500 stocks are down at least 20% from their highs, 41% are down more than 30%, and 17% are off by more than 50%. "A few names are carrying the entire stock market," strategists at the Kobeissi Letter rightly pointed out.

Yet despite the drawdowns underneath the surface of the S&P 500, the market is celebrating a milestone.

Investors are currently living in the 11th bull market since the 1950s , which is on track to become the seventh to complete at least four full years on Oct. 12, per data from Truist co-chief investment officer Keith Lerner.

Measured against every bull market dating back to the 1950s, the 119% advance sits near the middle of the pack, well below the 401% gain during the 2009 to 2020 cycle and the 582% gain from 1987 to 2000.

The historical average advance for a bull market in Lerner's measurement period is 184%. Of the 10 prior bull markets, six lasted longer than four years.

articles.title: Oil gains on Middle East tensions, growing doubts of 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine
articles.summary: Oil prices jumped as Ukraine said Russia must adhere to President Trump's energy ceasefire.
articles.body:
Oil prices rose on Monday amid growing doubts over a Russia-Ukraine "energy ceasefire" announced by President Trump over the weekend.

Meanwhile, Middle East tensions expanded after Saudi Arabia said it had suffered its deadliest attack since the outbreak of the US-Iran war, adding to worries over further supply disruptions.

Brent crude ( BZ=F ) rose to $106 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) dropped to $93 a barrel.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday said strikes against Russia would continue if Moscow doesn't agree to the energy truce. Trump had said earlier that both sides had agreed not to hit either side's energy infrastructure.

"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," Trump posted on Sunday morning. "Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"

The announcement initially raised hopes of improved global energy supplies.

Higher energy costs are adding to expectations that the Federal Reserve will maintain its tightening stance to curb inflation. The market fully priced in a 25 basis point Federal Reserve rate increase in December.

On Friday, President Trump announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to release diesel supplies to the US and the global market.

The administration has been looking for ways to ease high energy costs ahead of November's midterm elections.

However, continued tensions in the Middle East, along with recent shut-ins near the Gulf Coast due to Hurricane Isaias, could remain volatile in the coming days.

articles.title: Starbucks confirms it is not buying Chipotle
articles.summary: Starbucks squashes rumors on Chipotle acquisition.
articles.body:
Starbucks ( SBUX ) does not plan to acquire Chipotle ( CMG ), the company confirmed on Monday, quashing the vision of a breakfast burrito paired with a cortado.

"As a matter of policy, we don't comment on rumors and speculation, but we want to be clear we are not buying Chipotle," a spokesperson told Yahoo Finance.

The company added in a statement that it is "laser focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy" and generating momentum ahead of its next quarterly results on Oct. 29 after the closing bell.

Starbucks' statement follows a Financial Times report last Thursday that the coffee giant explored a takeover of the burrito chain .

The rumor mill leaned into the story given Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol's close ties with the burrito chain. Niccol was Chipotle's CEO for six years and spent time at food conglomerate Yum! Brands ( YUM ) prior to that.

Since Niccol announced his departure from Chipotle, the stock has fallen more than 25%. In its latest quarter, same-store sales increased 2.2%, but food safety concerns hit the tail end of the quarter amid a potential Salmonella outbreak in Chipotle's supply chain.

If Starbucks had proceeded with the takeover, it would still be the largest restaurant acquisition in history. Some analysts tried to wrap their heads around how the two could mutually benefit each other .

"There are no obvious revenue synergies between the two brands, although perhaps opportunities exist in shared loyalty ecosystems, cross-brand product placements (i.e., Starbucks Refreshers with your Barbacoa Burrito Bowl), or expanding Chipotle's licensed international business more quickly through Starbucks' existing relationships," William Blair analyst Sharon Zackfia wrote to clients.

TD Cowen's Andrew Charles called it "a low-probability" event from the start.

"Our initial reaction is skepticism," he wrote in a note. "While there is plausibility given CEO Brian Niccol's history at Chipotle, a transaction of this size would likely distract from Starbucks' ongoing turnaround. This is on top of the cost and integration risk."

Last month, Starbucks shared plans to close 250 stores in the US and Canada, reducing its store count by roughly 1%. The news followed a strong third quarter, indicating that Niccol's turnaround plan was making progress.

Starbucks posted same-store sales growth of 7.9%, more than the 5.7% growth Wall Street expected, according to Bloomberg data, and above the 6.2% jump seen in Q2. Last year, the company saw a 2% decline in overall same-store sales growth in the third quarter.

articles.title: Social Security COLA 2027 latest forecast: See how much your benefits could rise
articles.summary: Experts are forecasting a 3.5% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027. Here's how that could impact the average Social Security payment.
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

The Social Security Administration will announce the official annual cost-of-living-adjustment (COLA) on Wednesday, Oct. 14, following the Bureau of Labor Statistics' release of September inflation data. Recipients will receive their personalized notices detailing their new benefit amounts in December.

According to a forecast from The Senior Citizens League (TSCL), the adjustment is projected to be 3.5% in 2027, down 0.1 percentage point from last month's forecast of 3.6%.

This forecast is also in line with projections from Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare policy analyst. Johnson told CNBC that the Social Security COLA for 2027 could be 3.5%, though the final figure could change due to volatile oil prices.

"The biggest thing we're watching with the COLA announcement coming are short-term shocks to the economy that push inflation way up or down in the next 30 days," TSCL executive director Shannon Benton said in a statement. "Of the three CPI-W figures used to calculate the COLA, two are already in."

If TSCL's projections are correct, a 3.5% COLA would boost the average retiree's monthly check by $67.90, from $1,940.08 to $2,007.98.

COLAs are based on increases in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). CPI-Ws are calculated on a monthly basis by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

The point of these adjustments is to ensure that Social Security benefits keep up with inflation.

This forecast comes after the release of August's Consumer Price Index (CPI), which showed a 3.4% year-over-year increase in consumer prices. Gas prices spiked 3.9% last month amid the ongoing war between the U.S. and Iran, and "core" inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3% month over month.

If TSCL's projection holds, it would mark the largest COLA increase in four years. Still — experts say it could be a letdown for seniors.

"No matter if the COLA announcement comes in slightly higher or slightly lower than our prediction, seniors will probably end up disappointed in the long run," said Benton. "The reality is that older Americans allocate their budgets differently than people still in the workforce, so inflation hits them differently. The CPI-W captures the experience of urban wage earners, which doesn't represent the average senior's budget."

A COLA effective for December of the current year is equal to the percentage increase (if any) in the CPI-W from the average for the third quarter of the current year to the average for the third quarter of the last year in which a COLA became effective. If there is an increase, it must be rounded to the nearest tenth of one percent. If there is no increase, or if the rounded increase is zero, there is no COLA for the year.

You can find out exactly how much your benefits will increase by creating an account on SSA.gov . After verifying your account, you'll be able to get an estimate of your retirement benefits and see how those benefits may change depending on your retirement age.

You can also crunch the numbers yourself and calculate your new Social Security benefit by multiplying the percentage increase by your current monthly benefit amount.

Say you're receiving $2,071, which is around the current average monthly benefit for retirees according to the SSA. When multiplied by the estimated COLA of 3.5% or 0.035%, you can expect a monthly benefit of about $2,143.48 — about a $72 increase.

articles.title: Why bank stocks shocked everyone by getting thrashed
articles.summary: Share prices across the entire banking sector have flat-out crashed, placing many top names in correction territory.
articles.body:
So much for bank stocks loving higher interest rates.

That old saw is being completely ignored ahead of earnings from big banks, which kick off this week with numbers out of JPMorgan ( JPM ), Bank of America ( BAC ), Goldman Sachs ( GS ), and Wells Fargo ( WFC ).

Share prices across the entire banking sector have flat-out crashed, placing many top names in correction territory — down 10% from their highs.

Over the past month, JPMorgan has shed 6%, Citigroup is down 6.5%, Wells Fargo is off 7%, Morgan Stanley ( MS ) is down 11%, Goldman Sachs is down 12%, and Bank of America is down 13%.

Even the KBW Nasdaq Bank Index ( ^BKX ), which tracks the 24 publicly traded US banking stocks, is now down more than 14% from its August peak.

"This means if the Bank Index continues to drop even with the S&P 500 hitting new highs, it could be a major warning sign for the US stock market," the team at the Macro Paper said.

Pros point to a few factors for the surprise sell-off despite the US economy continuing to chug along.

The first is what may be a less lucrative market for deals in the near term amid concerns about sky-high valuations on tech companies. To that end, it's unlikely OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) IPO will happen this year, and others thought to be coming to market are on pause.

"Indeed Oura's delayed IPO while the generational OpenAI offering expected this year being pushed back to 2027 has raised fears of a deteriorating funding environment. Deposit competition from AI offerings maximizing cash yields has also weighed on sentiment," Evercore ISI strategist Julian Emanuel said.

The other issue at play is the perception that new technology will meaningfully disrupt the financial services space in the years to come. For example, companies such as Robinhood ( HOOD ) and Coinbase ( COIN ) have unveiled new agentic trading capabilities for their customers. (Disclosure: Yahoo Finance has a partnership with Coinbase.)

Emanuel explained, "Focus this reporting season will first be placed intently on Financials, whose recent underperformance has been striking. The sector has historically been a beneficiary of higher interest rates (supporting net interest margins) but has fallen precipitously since yields have spiked above 5% and as some perceive a threat to financials' margins with the debut of consumer AI Agent Muse."

Microsoft ( MSFT ) stock climbed higher in early morning trading on Monday, helping propel the company's market capitalization above the $4 trillion mark, joining the likes of Nvidia ( NVDA ), Apple ( AAPL ), and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), which have also eclipsed the number .
