articles.title: Iran sets crosshairs on ‘US-UAE’ oil shuttle out of Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: The IRGC is hitting more ships allegedly part of a shuttle operation to move crude oil beyond the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have signalled they intend to disrupt an Arab-operated and United States-assisted shuttle system that has enabled more energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Israel war on Iran.

With the US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place and sanctions tightening, Tehran has said it will pursue military and diplomatic efforts to put pressure on Washington to submit to its demands regarding reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

This strategic waterway, through which roughly a fifth of global oil and gas flowed before the war, has been largely closed to shipping following Iranian attacks since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28.

But the US Navy has reportedly opened up a route so Gulf states can export oil and other commodities amid an energy crisis.

Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei responded on Sunday night, saying the shuttle system is now an explicit target for Tehran.

Rezaei claimed that the US Central Command, with the assistance of the United Arab Emirates military, was using smaller vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers. He claimed Iran had been striking five or six participating vessels nightly for weeks.

“You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iran’s control, and we manage it,” he asserted.

This appeared to be a taunt aimed at US President Donald Trump, who has hailed energy exports at times reaching pre-war levels over recent weeks.

Rezaei appeared to give the impression that Iran wants to have lasting authority over Hormuz, and promised a harsh response if Iran’s energy and civilian infrastructure were attacked again.

His threats appeared aimed at Arab regional states, with a warning that digital infrastructure could be targeted. Rezaei threatened US-linked cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities in the UAE and around the Strait of Hormuz.

Rezaei also accused Saudi Arabia of helping the US move oil around Iran’s restrictions. But he did not threaten a direct attack against Riyadh – which is currently being targeted by Yemen’s Tehran-aligned Houthis.

In early September, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) threatened tankers at ports and anchorages in Kuwait and Bahrain, citing US attacks on Iranian tankers . It accused both countries of complicity through hosting US armed forces.

Iran has claimed the US accepted some of Tehran’s seven conditions for the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and ending the war. But Tehran insists that a deal will only materialise when all its demands are met.

Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the Crisis Group, said this reflects Tehran’s apparent assessment that it is under no immediate pressure to reach an agreement with the US since its pressure in the Hormuz has a global impact.

“The question, however, is whether Tehran is overestimating its ability to sustain this pressure, given the growing economic costs of the confrontation for Iran itself,” Azizi wrote on X.

The system involves very large crude carriers (VLCCs) and smaller vessels coordinating with the US military to load crude oil at Arab ports and use southern corridors near the coast of Oman to exit the strait.

Vessels often switch off their transponders and travel at night to minimise the risk of being targeted by the Iranians. After ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, some of the shuttles come back to load more.

Multiple vessels were targeted overnight Sunday to Monday, including two outbound tankers and one in anchorage near Oman’s port city of Sohar, where ship-to-ship transfers are allegedly being conducted.

Other vessels were targeted by projectiles last week, indicating that attacks have extended beyond the Strait of Hormuz to target the shuttle system.

The IRGC has also increasingly driven a narrative that naval mines, believed to have been planted across the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the war, pose a serious threat to vessels attempting to navigate the waterway without coordinating with Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority.

The IRGC said three tankers suffered major damage over the weekend after being struck by mines. It also released footage of one ship ablaze that is said to have been struck by a mine, although the footage did not appear to show a mine going off.

The shuttle system has provided Arab national oil companies with a way out of Hormuz via the southern corridor near Oman.

Michelle Wiese Bockmann, a London-based senior maritime intelligence analyst at Windward, said this system has proven highly effective.

“Under international maritime law, which underpins 11 billion tonnes of seaborne trade annually, vessels have what’s called the right of transit passage,” Bockmann told Al Jazeera. “So, what Oman has done is allow vessels to go through under international maritime law, but they have had US military assistance.”

Tehran says shipping will be disrupted so long as the US continues its choking naval blockade against Iran, which has also stepped up its efforts to counter efforts by Arab states to export oil. At least 15 ships are believed to have been targeted in October so far, according to Winward.

“The more effective the route has become in facilitating the transport of oil and gas, the less leverage Iran has over Hormuz, and more attacks we are seeing on vessels that are using that southern corridor,” Bockmann said.

Windward’s data shows 31 ships transited the Strait of Hormuz daily in the final week of September. This was considerably lower than the 138 before the war.

Eighty-seven percent of the 45 ships targeted by Iran during the third quarter of 2026 were tankers.

Around 47 percent belonged to Gulf Arab energy companies’ national shipping fleets, Windward noted, and 93 percent of the strikes took place in the Strait of Hormuz. Most attacks targeted vessels transiting the southern corridor with their transponders turned off.

These attacks have contributed to a massive increase in freight costs. Freight represented 25-30 percent of Gulf crude’s cost, versus just 1 to 3 percent before the war, according to Windward. National oil companies have resorted to offering discounts of up to $35 per barrel below official selling prices.

The main reason for the rise is a shortage of tankers willing to make the dangerous crossing. Between 15 and 20 percent of very large crude carriers (VLCCs) are tied up with an inefficient logistics system that relies on shuttle transfers, complicated by escalating attacks and exposure at loading ports and anchorages.

“This is having cascading impacts for all vessel classes on freight and values across the world,” Bockmann said.

articles.title: 'I'm going to keep winning by innovating': Ring founder Jamie Siminoff isn't sweating Apple's smart home push
articles.summary: Ring founder Jamie Siminoff says he's simply heads down in his role as inventor and leader at Ring, where he is now an employee of Ring owner Amazon
articles.body:
Listen and subscribe to Power Players with Brian Sozzi on Apple Podcasts , Amazon Music , Spotify , YouTube , or wherever you find your favorite podcasts.

Ring founder Jamie Siminoff said he does not have a picture of new Apple ( AAPL ) CEO John Ternus in his office as a motivational tool.

He is simply heads down in his role as inventor and leader at Ring, where he is now an employee of Ring owner Amazon ( AMZN ).

"I'm going to keep winning by innovating and coming out with products that no one has ever seen that deliver huge value and that people want to reward me because it delivers them value. They're going to reward me by buying it. I'm just going to keep doing that. Keep my head down," Siminoff said in a new episode of the Power Players with Brian Sozzi podcast (video above; listen in below).

Siminoff is fresh off debuting Ring's first smart lock, which features a first-of-its-kind power dial that lets you recharge the lock by hand if the battery dies.

It also eliminates the standard door key in four ways: a fingerprint reader, a keypad, the Ring app, or via Alexa. The new smart lock will integrate with Ring and Amazon devices and will be available in early 2027.

And it's likely to go toe-to-toe with a reinvigorated Apple in the smart home market .

Apple is widely expected to anchor its upcoming Welcome Home event this week with the reveal of its long-rumored — and well behind the curve — dedicated smart home display hub .

The hub could include a video doorbell, a smart lock, and a smart thermostat, developed through a strategic partnership with LG Electronics ( 066570.KS ), in a direct challenge to Amazon's Ring and Google's ( GOOG , GOOGL ) Nest.

Apple is finding a formidable competitor in Siminoff and Ring.

This success story began in Siminoff's garage with a product he called Doorbot. He pitched Doorbot on Shark Tank in 2013, seeking $700,000 for a 10% stake.

Surprisingly, he walked away empty-handed after all investors rejected the opportunity — a decision that Kevin "Mr. Wonderful" O'Leary later called one of Shark Tank's biggest misses.

Siminoff went on to rename the product Ring, turning it into one of the most ubiquitous home consumer products. He sold the business to tech giant Amazon in 2018 for $1.15 billion.

Ring has since developed a host of connected security products, from floodlights to new iterations of its iconic connected doorbell.

Siminoff left Amazon in 2023, only to return in early 2025 to lead its suite of security products.

He said he has been tasked with taking the connected security platform to new heights by tapping into the power of AI while driving a more efficient business.

articles.title: Nvidia, AMD, Google, and Meta team up on global blueprint for data center design
articles.summary: Nvidia is teaming up with AMD, Google, Meta to establish standards related to data center construction.
articles.body:
Nvidia ( NVDA ) is joining rival AMD ( AMD ) along with partners Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) and Meta ( META ) to establish a new open specification for data center design.

Called the Open Data Center Specification v0.7, the standard serves as a blueprint for building data centers, covering everything from the physical layout of the buildings to cooling and power architecture.

The chip giant also said it's teaming with Google, Meta, and Microsoft ( MSFT ) to create the OCP Grid Resilience Specification , which serves as a standard for how data centers respond to power disruptions, ensuring they can rapidly return to full operation.

According to Nvidia, the two specifications provide everyone from system makers to colocation providers and data center operators with a set of predefined templates for building data centers without having to contend with a slew of different customer designs.

Data centers are incredibly complex facilities that require large amounts of power and cooling to keep the chips inside from overheating and failing. And adding custom designs and quirks can slow construction timelines.

Open standards could change that, allowing builders to bring new data centers online faster. And the faster data centers go up, the more chips, systems, and networking components Nvidia can sell.

At the same time, data centers are facing increasing pushback from communities across the US, with some towns and counties imposing moratoriums or outright bans to stop companies from building them.

New York has enacted a statewide, one-year moratorium on data center construction, and Texas has halted new projects until it can determine the impact that connecting more power-hungry sites will have on its electrical grid.

President Trump has pushed back against any resistance to data centers, saying they'll be moneymakers for states.

articles.title: 'AI 3.0 is the interface': Salesforce stock pops on BoA upgrade
articles.summary: Salesforce stock rose after Bank of America analysts changed their minds about the SaaSpocalypse.
articles.body:
Salesforce stock ( CRM ) rose as much as 5% Monday morning after Bank of America upgraded it to Buy from Underperform after deciding that previous worries that AI would cut Salesforce out of enterprise software were overdone.

BofA analyst Tal Liani raised his price target to $285 from $160, a 78% increase. The new target sits about 24% above Friday's close of $229.13. The stock was up about 2% shortly before 10 a.m. ET.

"If AI 1.0 was the model, AI 2.0 was the agent, then AI 3.0 is the interface," Liani wrote in a note to clients Monday.

That shift was the risk BofA had flagged earlier: As workers hand tasks to AI assistants, they may stop opening Salesforce apps at all. That fear hammered many software stocks for a stretch, though the group has rallied sharply since the end of June , with Salesforce among the top performers.

Conversations with chief information officers and other market participants changed BofA's call. Large companies, the note said, are unlikely to replace the platforms that house their business logic, data, workflows, and compliance frameworks.

"If anything, AI should deepen dependence on these platforms," Liani wrote.

BofA argued that Salesforce covers all four layers a company needs to put AI to work: data (Informatica and Data 360), applications (Sales Cloud and Service Cloud), agents (Agentforce), and the interface (Slack, Claudeforce).

The "SaaSpocalypse" narrative, the firm added, "overstates the extent to which losing the user interface translates into losing platform value for Salesforce."

BofA also sees early signs that growth will pick up, including strong growth in net new annual order value, a bookings measure, and faster gains at Slack. It raised its forecasts for subscription and support revenue growth in fiscal 2028 and 2029 to 10.4% and 10.5%, from 9.9% and 10.2%.

The main near-term risk, according to the note, is that companies adopt AI more slowly than expected, since Salesforce's AI revenue is still small.

articles.body: US stocks rose on Monday morning as investors geared up for big bank earnings on Tuesday and watched energy markets for geopolitical developments. articles.title: Social Security commissioner predicts program will last ‘for another 90 years’

It’ll be around for another 90 years,” Bisignano said on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.” The SSA will release its annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) on Wednesday, after the Bureau…
articles.body:
Frank Bisignano, the commissioner of the Social Security Administration (SSA), said Monday the program will last another 90 years.

“This is a long journey. It’s 90 years old. It’ll be around for another 90 years,” Bisignano said on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.”

The SSA will release its annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) on Wednesday, after the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reports data for September inflation, as measured by the consumer price index (CPI).

For this year, the SSA increased benefits for the roughly 75 million recipients of Social Security by 2.8 percent. The Senior Citizens League projects the program’s COLA for 2027 will be 3.5 percent, which would be the fourth-highest adjustment since 2008.

That would boost the average monthly Social Security benefit check, which the federal government first sent in 1937 , from $1,941.76 to $2,009.72, based on August data from the SSA.

“People are very, very grateful for it, and they look forward to it,” Bisignano said Monday of the annual COLA.

Annual inflation, as measured by the CPI, was 3.4 percent in August . The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland projects the BLS will measure year-over-year inflation as 3.6 percent in September.

Earlier this year, Bisignano and other Trump administration officials said Social Security’s Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund will cover only 78 percent of scheduled benefits starting in the early 2030s.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have since proposed multiple solutions for the program’s impending funding shortfall , while President Trump reiterated his view last week that the federal government should invest Social Security’s trust fund in the stock market.

“I wanted to ride with Social Security being fully invested in the stock market in the first month of my first year,” Trump said in the Oval Office during an event to tout his administration’s investment accounts for children.

“Had we done that, Social Security right now would be the richest entity anywhere in the world. … I was met with tremendous criticism by the Democrats and some Republicans, because … they felt it was risky,” the president added.
